outline.point: Variables, primitive data types, and basic input/output (cin/cout)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a program that reads two integers from input and prints their sum, difference, and product.

outline.point: Operators and control flow: if/else, switch, for, while loops
outline.practicePrompt: Write a program that prints the FizzBuzz sequence from 1 to 50 using a for loop and if/else.

outline.point: Functions: declaration, parameters, return values, pass-by-value vs pass-by-reference
outline.practicePrompt: Write a function that swaps two integers using pass-by-reference, and another that does the same using a pointer, then explain the difference.

outline.point: Arrays and strings basics (declaration, traversal, common string functions)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a program that reads a string and reverses it in place without using a built-in reverse function.

outline.point: Pointers and dynamic memory allocation basics (new/delete)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a small program that dynamically allocates an array of 10 integers with new, fills it, and frees it with delete[]; explain what happens if you forget delete[].

outline.point: Standard Template Library (STL) basics: vector, pair, and iterating containers
outline.practicePrompt: Write a program that stores 5 numbers in a std::vector, sorts it, and prints the result.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: difference between stack and heap memory, and common pitfalls (dangling pointers, memory leaks)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain out loud the difference between stack and heap memory in C++, and describe one scenario that causes a memory leak.

outline.point: What time and space complexity measure, and why they matter
outline.practicePrompt: Explain in plain language why two programs that produce the same output can have very different running times as input size grows.

outline.point: Big-O notation: best case, worst case, and average case
outline.practicePrompt: For a linear search function, state its best-case and worst-case time complexity and explain the scenario that produces each.

outline.point: Common complexity classes: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n)
outline.practicePrompt: Rank these five complexities from fastest to slowest growing and give one real algorithm example for each: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2).

outline.point: Analyzing time complexity of simple code (single loops, nested loops)
outline.practicePrompt: Look at 3 short code snippets (single loop, nested loop, loop with a halving step) and write down the Big-O of each.

outline.point: Space complexity analysis, including recursion stack space
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why a recursive factorial function uses O(n) space even though it doesn't declare any arrays.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: comparing two solutions to the same problem by time-space trade-off (e.g. brute force vs hashmap-based approach)
outline.practicePrompt: For the 'two sum' problem, compare the brute-force O(n^2) solution to the hashmap-based O(n) solution and explain the time-space trade-off out loud.

outline.point: Classes and objects: defining a class, creating objects, member variables and methods
outline.practicePrompt: Define a 'Book' class with title, author, and price attributes, and a method that prints the book's details, then create two Book objects.

outline.point: Constructors and destructors
outline.practicePrompt: Add a parameterized constructor to your Book class and a destructor that prints a message when a Book object is destroyed.

outline.point: Encapsulation: access modifiers (public/private/protected), getters and setters
outline.practicePrompt: Make the Book class's attributes private and add getter/setter methods, then explain why direct access was restricted.

outline.point: Inheritance: base and derived classes, code reuse through 'is-a' relationships
outline.practicePrompt: Create a base class 'Animal' with a method makeSound(), and derived classes 'Dog' and 'Cat' that override it, then instantiate and call each.

outline.point: Polymorphism: compile-time (function/operator overloading) vs runtime (function overriding via virtual functions)
outline.practicePrompt: Write one example of function overloading (same function name, different parameters) and one example of runtime polymorphism using a base class pointer calling an overridden virtual function.

outline.point: Abstraction: abstract classes and interfaces
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between abstraction and encapsulation using your Animal class example, and identify which part of your code demonstrates abstraction.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: encapsulation vs abstraction, and overloading vs overriding — the two comparisons interviewers ask most
outline.practicePrompt: Explain out loud, with one example each, the difference between encapsulation and abstraction, and the difference between function overloading and overriding.

outline.point: Composition over inheritance, and a first look at SOLID principles
outline.practicePrompt: Describe a scenario where you would prefer composition ('has-a') over inheritance ('is-a'), and name one SOLID principle you could apply to improve it.

outline.point: Array representation, traversal, and time complexity of access/insert/delete
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why array access is O(1) but inserting an element in the middle of an array is O(n).

outline.point: Two-pointer technique on arrays (opposite ends and same-direction pointers)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a two-pointer solution to check if a sorted array has two numbers that sum to a target value.

outline.point: Sliding window technique for subarray/substring problems
outline.practicePrompt: Write a sliding-window solution that finds the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of size k.

outline.point: Prefix sums for range-sum queries
outline.practicePrompt: Build a prefix-sum array for a given array and use it to answer 3 range-sum queries in O(1) each.

outline.point: String traversal, common string operations (reverse, palindrome check, substring)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a function that checks whether a given string is a palindrome, ignoring case and spaces.

outline.point: In-place array manipulation (reversing, rotating an array without extra space)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a function that rotates an array to the right by k steps in-place, without using extra array space.

outline.point: Multi-dimensional arrays (2D array traversal, matrix basics)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a function that transposes a square matrix in place.

outline.point: What recursion is: base case, recursive case, and the call stack
outline.practicePrompt: Trace, step by step on paper, the call stack for computing factorial(4) recursively.

outline.point: Writing basic recursive functions (factorial, Fibonacci, sum of digits)
outline.practicePrompt: Write recursive functions for factorial and Fibonacci, then identify which calls are repeated in the Fibonacci case.

outline.point: Recursion on arrays and strings (reverse a string recursively, check palindrome recursively)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a recursive function that reverses a string and another that checks if a string is a palindrome.

outline.point: Backtracking basics: explore, check constraint, backtrack pattern
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the 'choose, explore, un-choose' backtracking pattern out loud using the subsets-generation problem as an example.

outline.point: Classic backtracking problems: generating subsets and permutations
outline.practicePrompt: Write a backtracking function that generates all subsets of a given array, and another that generates all permutations of a string.

outline.point: Backtracking with constraints (N-Queens or Sudoku-style problems) at a conceptual level
outline.practicePrompt: Explain how the N-Queens problem uses backtracking to prune invalid placements early, without necessarily coding the full solution.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: recursion vs iteration trade-offs and stack overflow risk
outline.practicePrompt: Explain when you would prefer an iterative solution over a recursive one, referencing stack overflow risk on deep recursion.

outline.point: Linear search and binary search (iterative and recursive)
outline.practicePrompt: Implement binary search both iteratively and recursively on a sorted array, and verify both give the same result.

outline.point: Basic O(n^2) sorts: bubble sort, selection sort, insertion sort
outline.practicePrompt: Implement bubble sort and insertion sort on a small array by hand-tracing 2 passes each before coding them.

outline.point: Efficient O(n log n) sorts: merge sort and quicksort
outline.practicePrompt: Implement merge sort, and trace through the partition step of quicksort on a 6-element array by hand.

outline.point: Comparing sorting algorithms: stability, in-place vs extra space, best/worst case
outline.practicePrompt: Explain what a 'stable' sort means, and state which of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort are stable.

outline.point: Binary search on the answer / applying binary search to non-obvious problems
outline.practicePrompt: Use binary search to find the first occurrence of a target value in a sorted array with duplicates.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: when to choose quicksort vs merge sort in practice, and built-in sort function complexity
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why quicksort's worst case is O(n^2) but it's still often used in practice over merge sort.

outline.point: Singly linked list structure: node, head, traversal
outline.practicePrompt: Implement a singly linked list class with insert-at-head and print/traverse methods.

outline.point: Insertion and deletion at head, tail, and a given position
outline.practicePrompt: Add insert-at-tail and delete-at-position methods to your linked list class and test each with a 5-node list.

outline.point: Reversing a linked list (iterative and recursive)
outline.practicePrompt: Write both an iterative and a recursive function to reverse a singly linked list.

outline.point: Fast and slow pointer technique: detecting a cycle, finding the middle node
outline.practicePrompt: Implement Floyd's cycle detection (fast/slow pointer) to detect if a linked list has a cycle.

outline.point: Doubly linked lists and circular linked lists (conceptual differences from singly linked lists)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the trade-off of a doubly linked list (extra pointer per node) versus a singly linked list, and one use case for a circular linked list.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: merging two sorted linked lists, and array vs linked list trade-offs
outline.practicePrompt: Write a function that merges two sorted linked lists into one sorted linked list, then explain when you'd choose a linked list over an array.

outline.point: Stack (LIFO): push, pop, peek, and implementing a stack using an array or linked list
outline.practicePrompt: Implement a stack using an array with push, pop, and peek operations, and test it with a sequence of operations.

outline.point: Queue (FIFO): enqueue, dequeue, and circular queue basics
outline.practicePrompt: Implement a queue using an array (or two stacks) with enqueue and dequeue operations.

outline.point: Classic stack application: valid parentheses / balanced brackets checking
outline.practicePrompt: Write a function using a stack that checks whether a string of brackets like '{[()]}' is balanced.

outline.point: Classic stack application: evaluating postfix expressions or implementing undo functionality (conceptual)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain how a stack could be used to implement the 'undo' feature of a text editor.

outline.point: Priority queues and heaps: min-heap/max-heap concept and use cases
outline.practicePrompt: Explain what a min-heap guarantees about its root element, and describe one real use case (e.g. finding the k smallest elements).

outline.point: Interview-favorite: stack vs queue vs deque comparison, and implementing a queue using two stacks
outline.practicePrompt: Implement a queue using two stacks and explain the amortized time complexity of the dequeue operation.

outline.point: What a hash function and hash table are, and why average-case lookup is O(1)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in plain language, how a hash function maps a key to an array index, and why two different keys can end up at the same index.

outline.point: Collision handling: chaining vs open addressing (conceptual overview)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between chaining and open addressing as two ways to resolve hash collisions.

outline.point: Using hash maps/sets in practice (insert, lookup, delete, iterate)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a function that uses a hash set to check whether an array contains any duplicate values.

outline.point: Frequency counting pattern using a hash map (a very common interview pattern)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a function that finds the first non-repeating character in a string using a hash map of character frequencies.

outline.point: The 'two sum' pattern: solving array-pair problems in O(n) using a hash map instead of O(n^2) brute force
outline.practicePrompt: Solve the 'two sum' problem (find two numbers that add up to a target) in O(n) time using a hash map.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: hash table vs balanced BST for lookups, and worst-case degradation of hash tables
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why hash table lookups are usually O(1) but can degrade to O(n) in the worst case, and when a balanced BST might be preferred instead.

outline.point: Tree terminology: root, node, leaf, height, depth; binary tree structure
outline.practicePrompt: Draw a binary tree with 7 nodes and label its root, leaves, height, and the depth of two specific nodes.

outline.point: Tree traversals: in-order, pre-order, post-order (recursive), and level-order (using a queue)
outline.practicePrompt: Implement in-order, pre-order, post-order, and level-order traversal on a small binary tree and verify the outputs by hand.

outline.point: Binary Search Tree (BST) properties and operations: insert, search, delete
outline.practicePrompt: Implement insert and search for a BST, then insert the sequence 50, 30, 70, 20, 40 and draw the resulting tree.

outline.point: Why in-order traversal of a BST gives sorted order, and how to validate a BST
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why in-order traversal of a valid BST always produces values in sorted order, then write a function to check if a binary tree is a valid BST.

outline.point: Height/balance concepts: balanced vs skewed trees, and why balance matters for performance (AVL trees at a conceptual level)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why a completely skewed BST behaves like a linked list, degrading search from O(log n) to O(n).

outline.point: Common tree interview problems: height of a tree, lowest common ancestor (LCA), diameter of a tree
outline.practicePrompt: Write a recursive function to find the height of a binary tree, then a function to find the lowest common ancestor of two given nodes.

outline.point: Heaps as a specialized tree: min-heap/max-heap operations (insert, extract-min/max) and heap sort at a conceptual level
outline.practicePrompt: Explain how a min-heap maintains its 'parent smaller than children' property after an insert, using the sift-up operation.

outline.point: Graph terminology and representations: adjacency list vs adjacency matrix
outline.practicePrompt: Represent the same small graph (5 nodes, 6 edges) as both an adjacency list and an adjacency matrix, and note the space trade-off.

outline.point: Breadth-First Search (BFS) using a queue
outline.practicePrompt: Implement BFS on a graph represented as an adjacency list and print the visiting order starting from a given node.

outline.point: Depth-First Search (DFS), recursive and iterative (using a stack)
outline.practicePrompt: Implement DFS both recursively and iteratively (with an explicit stack) on the same graph and compare the visiting order to BFS.

outline.point: Detecting cycles in a graph (directed and undirected, conceptually)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain how DFS can be used to detect a cycle in a directed graph using the concept of a 'recursion stack' / visiting states.

outline.point: Shortest path algorithms: BFS for unweighted graphs, Dijkstra's algorithm for weighted graphs (conceptual)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why BFS alone finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph but not in a weighted graph, and why Dijkstra's algorithm is needed instead.

outline.point: Topological sort and its use case (task scheduling with dependencies)
outline.practicePrompt: Implement a topological sort (using DFS or Kahn's algorithm) on a small directed acyclic graph representing task dependencies.

outline.point: Minimum Spanning Tree basics: Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms (conceptual)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, at a high level, the difference in approach between Prim's algorithm (grows from a node) and Kruskal's algorithm (sorts edges) for building a minimum spanning tree.

outline.point: What makes a problem suitable for DP: overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, using the Fibonacci sequence, what 'overlapping subproblems' means and why naive recursion recomputes the same values.

outline.point: Memoization (top-down DP): converting a recursive solution to use a cache
outline.practicePrompt: Take your recursive Fibonacci function and add memoization using an array or hash map, then compare its speed to the un-memoized version for n=35.

outline.point: Tabulation (bottom-up DP): building the solution iteratively from base cases
outline.practicePrompt: Rewrite the memoized Fibonacci solution as a bottom-up tabulation solution using a simple array.

outline.point: Classic 1D DP problems: climbing stairs, house robber, coin change
outline.practicePrompt: Solve the 'climbing stairs' problem (count ways to reach the top taking 1 or 2 steps) using tabulation.

outline.point: Classic 2D DP problems: 0/1 Knapsack, Longest Common Subsequence
outline.practicePrompt: Solve the 0/1 Knapsack problem using a 2D DP table for a small example with 4 items and a given capacity.

outline.point: Greedy algorithms: what makes a problem greedy-solvable, and how it differs from DP
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between a greedy approach and a DP approach, using the coin change problem as an example of where greedy can fail.

outline.point: Classic greedy problems: activity selection, fractional knapsack
outline.practicePrompt: Solve the activity selection problem (choosing the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals) using a greedy, sort-by-end-time approach.

outline.point: Relational model basics: tables, rows, columns, and schemas
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, with an example table, what a schema, a row, and a column represent in a relational database.

outline.point: Keys: primary key, foreign key, candidate key, composite key
outline.practicePrompt: Sketch two related tables (e.g. Orders and Customers) and label the primary key and foreign key that connects them.

outline.point: Normalization: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and why redundancy is removed
outline.practicePrompt: Take an unnormalized sample table with repeating groups and manually normalize it to 3NF, explaining each step.

outline.point: SQL basics: SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY (enough to query a database)
outline.practicePrompt: Write a query joining two tables (e.g. Orders and Customers) and grouping results to compute total order value per customer.

outline.point: Transactions and ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain each ACID property out loud using a bank fund-transfer example.

outline.point: Transaction isolation levels and the read phenomena they prevent: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads out loud, with one example of each, and state which isolation level prevents which.

outline.point: Indexes and why they speed up queries (conceptual, no need for B-tree internals yet)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain to a peer why a query filtering on an indexed column is faster than one filtering on a non-indexed column.

outline.point: What an OS does: process management, memory management, file systems, I/O (overview)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain in your own words the four main responsibilities of an operating system.

outline.point: Processes vs threads: definitions, memory sharing, and why threads are lighter-weight
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between a process and a thread, and give one reason multithreading improves performance over multiprocessing for some tasks.

outline.point: Process states and context switching
outline.practicePrompt: Draw the process state diagram (new, ready, running, waiting, terminated) and explain what triggers a transition from running to waiting.

outline.point: CPU scheduling algorithms: FCFS, SJF, Round Robin, Priority scheduling
outline.practicePrompt: Given a set of 4 processes with arrival and burst times, compute the average waiting time under FCFS and under Round Robin (with a given time quantum), and compare the results.

outline.point: Process synchronization: race conditions, critical sections, mutexes, and semaphores
outline.practicePrompt: Explain what a race condition is using a shared-bank-balance example, and describe how a mutex would prevent it.

outline.point: Deadlocks: the four necessary conditions, and prevention/avoidance at a conceptual level
outline.practicePrompt: List the four necessary conditions for a deadlock and explain how breaking just one of them prevents deadlock.

outline.point: Memory management: paging, segmentation, and virtual memory basics
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why virtual memory lets a program use more memory than is physically available, using the concept of paging.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: thrashing, and the difference between paging and segmentation
outline.practicePrompt: Explain what thrashing is and why it hurts system performance, then explain the difference between paging and segmentation.

outline.point: The OSI model: seven layers and what each one does
outline.practicePrompt: List the 7 OSI layers from bottom to top and give one protocol or concept that lives at each layer.

outline.point: The TCP/IP model and how it maps (loosely) to the OSI model
outline.practicePrompt: Explain why the TCP/IP model uses 4 layers instead of the OSI model's 7, and which OSI layers get merged.

outline.point: IP addressing basics: IPv4 vs IPv6, and what a subnet is (high level)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between IPv4 and IPv6 addressing, and why IPv6 was introduced.

outline.point: TCP vs UDP: connection-oriented vs connectionless, reliability trade-offs
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between TCP and UDP and give one real application that would use each (e.g. file transfer vs video streaming).

outline.point: The TCP three-way handshake
outline.practicePrompt: Draw and explain the three steps (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) of the TCP three-way handshake.

outline.point: DNS: how a domain name gets resolved to an IP address
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, step by step, what happens between typing a URL in a browser and the browser receiving the corresponding IP address.

outline.point: HTTP vs HTTPS, and a basic understanding of what happens when you 'type a URL and hit enter'
outline.practicePrompt: Practice explaining out loud, end to end, everything that happens from typing a URL to a webpage rendering in the browser.

outline.point: Why system design is asked even for freshers: thinking about scale and trade-offs, not just correctness
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in your own words, why an interviewer might ask a fresher to design something like a URL shortener instead of only asking DSA questions.

outline.point: Low-Level Design (LLD) basics: classes, relationships, and applying SOLID principles to a small system
outline.practicePrompt: Sketch the classes and relationships you would use to design a simple 'Parking Lot' system (e.g. ParkingLot, Slot, Vehicle classes).

outline.point: Common design patterns at an introductory level: Singleton, Factory, Observer
outline.practicePrompt: Explain in your own words when you'd use a Singleton pattern versus a Factory pattern, with one example each.

outline.point: Basic High-Level Design (HLD) vocabulary: load balancer, cache, database replication (conceptual only)
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, at a high level, what a load balancer does and why a system with a single server can become a bottleneck.

outline.point: Solving a simple LLD problem end-to-end (e.g. designing a Splitwise-like expense splitter or a vending machine)
outline.practicePrompt: Design the classes and core methods for a simple vending machine (states: idle, has-money, dispensing) on paper.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: how to structure a system design answer (clarify requirements, outline a simple design, discuss one trade-off) even for a fresher-level question
outline.practicePrompt: Practice a 5-minute mock answer to 'design a URL shortener' following the structure: clarify requirements → propose a simple design → mention one scaling trade-off.

outline.point: SELECT, FROM, WHERE — retrieving and filtering rows
outline.practicePrompt: Write 3 SELECT queries against a sample 'employees' table filtering by different conditions (equality, range, text match).

outline.point: Aggregate functions and GROUP BY/HAVING
outline.practicePrompt: Write a query that groups orders by customer and returns only customers whose total spend exceeds 10,000.

outline.point: JOINs: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL — combining rows from multiple tables
outline.practicePrompt: Given Orders and Customers tables, write an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN query and explain the difference in the row counts returned.

outline.point: Subqueries and Common Table Expressions (CTEs)
outline.practicePrompt: Rewrite a nested subquery as a CTE using the WITH clause and explain why the CTE version is easier to read.

outline.point: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE, and DROP, including which ones can be rolled back inside a transaction.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: writing a query for a 'find the Nth highest salary' style problem
outline.practicePrompt: Write a SQL query that finds the second-highest salary from an employees table without using a hardcoded LIMIT/OFFSET of exactly 1.

outline.point: What version control is and why it matters for collaborative development
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in your own words, one problem that would occur if a 3-person team edited the same codebase without version control.

outline.point: Basic Git workflow: init, add, commit, status, log
outline.practicePrompt: Initialize a Git repository, create a file, and make 3 separate commits, then view the history with git log.

outline.point: Branching: creating, switching, and merging branches
outline.practicePrompt: Create a new branch, make a change and commit it, then merge that branch back into main.

outline.point: Remote repositories: clone, push, pull, and working with GitHub/GitLab
outline.practicePrompt: Clone a public GitHub repository, make a small local change, commit it, and push it to a fork you own.

outline.point: Resolving merge conflicts
outline.practicePrompt: Deliberately create a merge conflict by editing the same line on two branches, then resolve it manually.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: git merge vs git rebase — what each does and when to use which
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between git merge and git rebase, and describe a scenario where you would use rebase over merge.

outline.point: How the client-server model works, and what a request/response cycle looks like
outline.practicePrompt: Explain, in your own words, the client-server model using a web browser and a website as the example.

outline.point: HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH) and status codes (2xx, 4xx, 5xx)
outline.practicePrompt: Match each HTTP method to a CRUD operation (Create/Read/Update/Delete), and explain the difference between a 404 and a 500 status code.

outline.point: REST API principles: resources, statelessness, and using URLs meaningfully
outline.practicePrompt: Design REST-style URL endpoints (with HTTP methods) for a simple 'books' resource supporting create, read, update, and delete.

outline.point: JSON as a data format for APIs
outline.practicePrompt: Write a JSON object representing a 'book' with title, author, and price fields, and validate it's syntactically correct.

outline.point: Making a basic API request and reading a response (using curl or a simple script)
outline.practicePrompt: Use curl (or a Python/JS script) to make a GET request to a public test API (e.g. a placeholder API) and print the JSON response.

outline.point: Interview-favorite: PUT vs PATCH, and what 'statelessness' means in REST
outline.practicePrompt: Explain the difference between PUT and PATCH, and explain what it means for a REST API to be 'stateless'.

outline.point: Number systems, percentages, and ratio/proportion basics
outline.practicePrompt: Solve 5 mixed percentage and ratio word problems within 10 minutes, timing yourself.

outline.point: Profit, loss, discount, and simple/compound interest problems
outline.practicePrompt: Solve 5 profit-and-loss and interest word problems, then re-derive each formula from first principles instead of memorizing it.

outline.point: Time, speed, distance and time & work problems
outline.practicePrompt: Solve 5 time-speed-distance problems and 5 time-and-work problems under a strict 15-minute timer.

outline.point: Permutations, combinations, and basic probability
outline.practicePrompt: Solve 3 permutation/combination problems and 3 basic probability problems.

outline.point: Logical reasoning: number/letter series, coding-decoding, blood relations, seating arrangements
outline.practicePrompt: Solve 3 number-series puzzles, 2 coding-decoding puzzles, and one seating-arrangement puzzle, checking answers against explanations afterward.

outline.point: Timed mock-test strategy for section-locked tests (TCS/Infosys/Wipro/AMCAT-style written rounds)
outline.practicePrompt: Take one 20-minute mock aptitude section and afterward write down which question types you should skip-and-return-to next time to save time.
